title: NumPy Introduction and Fundamentals
goal: Understand what NumPy is, why ndarrays beat Python lists for numeric work, and run your first array program.

topics.title: Create your first array
topics.body: np.array turns a Python list into an ndarray: one typed block of memory that supports vectorised maths, so mean() and shape are properties of the data rather than a loop you write.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40])
print(a, a.mean(), a.shape)

topics.title: Vectorised arithmetic
topics.body: An operation between an array and a scalar is applied to every element by compiled code, which is why `a * 2` needs no loop and returns a new array instead of mutating `a`.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(5)
print(a * 2)

topics.title: Typed memory, not a Python list
topics.body: Every ndarray has one dtype and a fixed itemsize, so nbytes tells you the real memory it occupies; a Python list stores pointers to separate objects and cannot answer that question.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a.dtype, a.itemsize, a.nbytes)

debug.title: Assignment inside print
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a += 1)
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
a += 1
print(a)

title: ndarray Fundamentals
goal: Read an array's shape, size, ndim, dtype and axes correctly before writing any operation on it.

topics.title: shape, size and ndim
topics.body: shape is one number per axis, size is the product of those numbers and ndim is how many axes exist — the three answers every shape error is really about.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
print(a.shape, a.size, a.ndim)

topics.title: dtype and itemsize
topics.body: The dtype decides how the bytes are interpreted and itemsize is the bytes per element; together they explain both the values you get and the memory you pay.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a.dtype, a.itemsize)

topics.title: Axis means the direction that is collapsed
topics.body: Reducing along axis 0 collapses rows (one result per column) and axis 1 collapses columns (one result per row); reading the output length tells you which axis was reduced.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(a.sum(axis=0), a.sum(axis=1))

debug.title: Reshape with the wrong element count
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(5).reshape(2, 3)
print(a)
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a)
debug.error: ValueError: cannot reshape array of size 5 into shape (2,3)

debug.title: An axis that does not exist
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 2))
print(a.sum(axis=2))
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 2))
print(a.sum(axis=1))
debug.error: AxisError: axis 2 is out of bounds for array of dimension 2

title: Array Creation and Initialization
goal: Create arrays with zeros, ones, full, arange, linspace, eye and diag, and pick the right constructor for a dataset.

topics.title: zeros, ones and full
topics.body: These allocate a new array of a given shape and fill it: zeros and ones are the common starting points, full repeats any value and needs the fill value explicitly.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.zeros(3), np.ones((2, 2)), np.full(3, 7))

topics.title: arange and linspace
topics.body: arange builds a range by step (the stop is excluded, like range) while linspace builds a fixed number of evenly spaced points including both ends — the safer choice for float grids.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.arange(0, 10, 2), np.linspace(0, 1, 3))

topics.title: Identity and diagonal matrices
topics.body: eye builds an identity matrix of any shape and diag builds a square matrix from a 1-D vector (or extracts the diagonal from a 2-D one).
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.eye(2), np.diag([1, 2]))

title: Data Types and Type Conversion
goal: Choose an explicit dtype, convert safely with astype and understand overflow, precision and memory cost.

topics.title: Converting with astype
topics.body: astype returns a NEW array with the requested dtype and truncates floats toward zero, so 1.7 becomes 1; the original array is untouched.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1.7, 2.9])
print(a.astype(int))

topics.title: Overflow is silent
topics.body: Integer dtypes wrap around on overflow instead of raising, so uint8 arithmetic can turn a large result into a small one — use a wider dtype when the range is not guaranteed.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([250], dtype=np.uint8)
print(a + 10)

topics.title: Smaller dtype, smaller memory
topics.body: float32 uses four bytes per element against eight for float64; choosing it deliberately cuts memory and bandwidth in half, at the cost of precision.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3], dtype=np.float32)
print(a.dtype, a.nbytes)

debug.title: A dtype name NumPy 2 removed
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
print(np.array([1, 2, 3], dtype='float'))
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
print(np.array([1, 2, 3], dtype=np.float64))

title: Array Indexing and Selection
goal: Select single values, rows and columns with basic, negative and fancy indexing, and read IndexError correctly.

topics.title: Positive and negative indexing
topics.body: Index 0 is the first element and -1 is the last, so negative indices count from the end without needing the length.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40])
print(a[0], a[-1])

topics.title: Rows and cells in 2-D
topics.body: The first index selects the row and the second the column; one index alone returns that whole row as a 1-D array.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
print(a[1, 2], a[0])

topics.title: Fancy indexing with an index array
topics.body: Passing a list of positions returns a new array of those elements in the order you asked for, which is how you reorder or sample rows.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40])
print(a[[0, 2]])

debug.title: Off-by-one on a 1-D array
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([10, 20, 30])
print(a[3])
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([10, 20, 30])
print(a[2])
debug.error: IndexError: index 3 is out of bounds for axis 0 with size 3

debug.title: Column index outside the row
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(a[0, 2])
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(a[0, 1])
debug.error: IndexError: index 2 is out of bounds for axis 1 with size 2
